title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt‑5‑mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation so the same generated candidate served as the baseline output for both conditions; the guarded GVR condition invoked up to one repair call only when the validator failed. Provider accounting shows 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly one repair invocation (total model calls used = 301). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300) was not supported. We diagnose the outcome as a ceiling effect combined with minimal GVR engagement (one repair call), provide artifact‑grounded diagnostics and representative validator traces, and release the full preregistration, execution manifest, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts for community reuse.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work shows LLMs can draft device configurations but also generate syntax, topology, or semantic errors unless paired with verification or human oversight. The NetOps community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple operational intent tasks and deterministic validators to support confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (generate–validate–repair, GVR) versus single‑pass generation.

This paper reports a sealed, preregistered, machine‑checkable experiment (study ac‑2026‑003‑prereg‑v1) that (1) constructs a synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) implements a deterministic snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) with explicit intent constraints and required sequences, and (3) runs a preregistered paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass generator (declared model gpt‑5‑mini) under a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task). The shared‑initial generation design forces any guarded improvement to derive from repair rather than sampling variance. Our primary confirmatory question was: under fixed seeds and the constrained repair budget, does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and technical studies document strong interest in LLMs for NetOps while highlighting persistent evaluation and safety gaps (coverage summarized in our evidence synthesis). Empirical work shows verifier‑assisted and repair workflows can reduce misconfigurations in limited settings but typically evaluate small task sets or require human adjudication. Studies on intent→configuration translation demonstrate feasible automated mapping techniques under controlled datasets but remain limited in scope. Security and failure analyses (prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucination) underscore operational risks for automated NetOps. Collectively, this literature motivates sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparisons that fix generator variance and focus on repair efficacy under constrained budgets. Our study responds directly to the identified gaps by producing a public, deterministic benchmark and validator and by preregistering a confirmatory paired test.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory hypothesis. We preregistered study ac‑2026‑003‑prereg‑v1 prior to execution. Primary hypothesis H1: a GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration defined the task bank, validator semantics, adapter/model configuration, sampling and repair budgets, exclusion rules, missingness plan, and the analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Task bank and canonical semantics. The deterministic task generator produced N=300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned equally across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 each). Each task encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), and an explicit required_sequence of atomic field changes required to satisfy the intent. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and represent abstract multi‑vendor device models; artifacts contain per‑task difficulty labels and canonical reference answers.

Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator applies snapshot semantics: it parses the candidate configuration, computes the resulting final_state, and accepts the candidate only if all declared constraints and required_sequence elements are satisfied. The validator returns a binary valid/invalid outcome plus enumerated violation codes and a normalized_configuration. The validator is intentionally conservative, deterministic, and stateless to produce machine‑checkable binary outcomes suitable for confirmatory inference.

Experimental design: shared‑initial, paired, constrained repair budget. To control generator variance we used a shared‑initial generation protocol: for each task we issued a single initial generation call whose output served as the baseline single‑pass candidate for both conditions. For the guarded GVR condition we ran the deterministic validator on this same shared candidate and permitted up to one automated repair call only if the validator failed (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This yields a paired comparison in which any guarded improvement must arise from the repair stage rather than from sampling different initial candidates. The preregistration planned up to 600 episodes (300 shared initial + up to 300 repairs) and required ≥270 completed pairs.

Model and adapter configuration; deterministic sampling semantics. The hosted adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) declared the model: declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" (requested_model = "gpt‑5‑mini"), provider = "openai_responses", max_output_tokens = 2000, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, reasoning_effort = "minimal", store = false, and temperature unset. The adapter operated in a deterministic sampling mode under the provider constraints so that the shared initial generation was repeatable under the recorded provider conditions. In practice, reproducing identical outputs requires access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and per‑call provider traces; reproducing identical behavior therefore depends on replaying archived provider traces or running against an identically configured provider endpoint.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. Execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider accounting recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. All provider call traces, raw results, task manifest, and per‑task validator traces are archived in the execution bundle and indexed in the execution manifest for audit and reuse.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. These aggregated results and the paired contingency table are published as analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv and condition_summary.csv) in the archived analysis bundle.

Representative per‑task diagnostics. The archived scoring JSONs for representative tasks (e.g., task‑000001 … task‑000006) show detailed validator traces including normalized_configuration, required_command_count, validation_before/after, and difficulty labels (examples: shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). These per‑task artifacts demonstrate that many tasks required multi‑step sequences and that the validator produced deterministic pass/fail outcomes with enumerated violation codes when applicable. The full raw results file contains the single instance where the baseline candidate failed while the guarded condition passed; the execution manifest indexes that episode and the associated repair provider trace so auditors can extract the exact discordant pair and the repair invocation trace from the archived bundle.

Power & sensitivity post‑hoc. The preregistered power routine targeted detection of a 0.10 absolute paired improvement at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. Observed baseline ≈0.997 violates those assumptions: with the observed margins the maximum achievable paired improvement is 0.00333, far smaller than the preregistered target. This arithmetic sensitivity observation follows directly from the observed contingency counts and the preregistered power routine and explains the lack of statistical significance for H1.
sections.discussion:
Null result interpretation and ceiling effect. The confirmatory null result should be interpreted in the narrow sense of the preregistered design: under the selected synthetic task bank, deterministic snapshot validator, shared‑initial generation, and constrained repair budget (≤1 repair), the GVR pipeline did not produce a materially higher pass rate. Two linked causes explain this finding. First, the shared generator under deterministic sampling produced correct candidates for 299/300 tasks, leaving almost no room for the preregistered detectable effect (0.10). Second, the guarded pipeline was triggered only on validator failures and thus executed the repair stage exactly once across 300 tasks; with so few repair events the experiment could not exercise repair efficacy at scale. Practically, these two factors create a ceiling effect that makes the preregistered test insensitive to repair value for this particular task set and adapter configuration.

Operational implications and benchmark design recommendations. Based on artifact‑grounded execution accounting and validator diagnostics we recommend concrete changes for future benchmark designs that aim to evaluate repair value: (A) increase task difficulty or include adversarial seeds to raise initial generator failure rates; (B) allow iterative/multi‑attempt repairs (≥1 repair per failed candidate) so repair can perform localized, corrective iterations; (C) evaluate multiple independent baseline generations per task to measure generator variance and to compare repair‑mediated selection strategies; (D) complement snapshot validators with stateful execution emulation that models temporal ordering and side effects. Each recommendation directly maps to documented run artifacts: 300 shared initial generations, a single repair invocation, and the distribution of difficulty labels in the task manifest.

Reproducibility and deterministic sampling. The run used deterministic adapter settings and archived per‑call provider traces, the model configuration, and the full raw results and task manifest in the execution bundle. Bit‑for‑bit reproduction requires replaying the archived provider traces or access to an identically configured provider/model release as recorded in the archived model_configuration artifact. The archived analysis artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv, condition_summary.csv, deterministic_reconciliation.json) provide machine‑checkable summaries that reproduce the numerical results reported here when executed against the same raw_results index.

Limitations and threats to validity. Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces snapshot constraints but omits vendor CLI idiosyncrasies and asynchronous runtime dynamics. External validity: tasks are synthetic and abstract multi‑vendor models (device counts 3–50); results do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks. Scope limits: only a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single validator version (v5.0) were evaluated. GVR engagement: with exactly one repair invocation across N=300 (provider stage_counts reported above), the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline, constraining conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets. Conclusion validity: near‑ceiling pass rates produce low discordance and thus low power to detect the preregistered effect size.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt‑5‑mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. Provider accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks, so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about the general effectiveness of automatic repair. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can extend this benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, and multi‑model comparisons to better evaluate when GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt‑5‑mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and the per‑call provider traces archived in the execution bundle.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and raw_results) and are authoritative for auditors.
